relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion clause, waiting period 4 years
decision_summary: Commission held that insurer failed to prove the policyholder had prior knowledge or diagnosis of diabetes before policy inception; mere post-hoc lab values were insufficient to establish non-disclosure.
successful_arguments: No documented diagnosis or treatment for diabetes existed before the policy start date
Insurer relied only on a single post-hospitalization lab report to infer a pre-existing condition, which the commission found insufficient
Policyholder had disclosed all conditions known to them at the time of application
key_evidence: Pre-policy medical records showing no diabetes diagnosis
Proposal form copy showing accurate disclosure of known conditions
Treating doctor's certificate on date of first diagnosis
source_citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Maharashtra, Consumer Case (illustrative, verify before public use)

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion clause, waiting period 4 years
decision_summary: Insurer's own empanelled doctor's pre-policy medical check-up report did not flag diabetes; commission held insurer cannot repudiate on a condition its own underwriting process missed.
successful_arguments: Insurer's pre-issuance medical examination did not detect or record diabetes
Burden of proof for non-disclosure lies with insurer and was not discharged
key_evidence: Insurer's own pre-policy medical examination report
Discharge summary from treating hospital
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Karnataka (illustrative, verify before public use)

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion clause, waiting period 3 years
decision_summary: Commission found clear documentary evidence (prior prescription records dated before policy inception) that policyholder was aware of and being treated for diabetes but did not disclose it in the proposal form.
failed_arguments: Policyholder argued they were unaware of the diagnosis, but pre-policy pharmacy records and a treating physician's prescription pre-dating the policy contradicted this
Argument that the condition was 'mild and unremarkable' did not overcome the non-disclosure finding
key_evidence: Pre-policy prescription dated 8 months before policy inception, explicitly for diabetes management
source_citation: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (illustrative, verify before public use)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for joint replacement surgery
decision_summary: Waiting period clause was validly applied and upheld, but commission directed partial payment for the portion of treatment (diagnostics, medication) not directly tied to the excluded surgical procedure.
successful_arguments: Ancillary treatment costs unrelated to the specific excluded procedure should be assessed separately
failed_arguments: Argument that the waiting period clause itself was unconscionable was rejected — it was clearly disclosed and IRDAI-compliant
key_evidence: Itemized hospital bill separating surgical and non-surgical costs
Policy document with waiting period schedule
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Tamil Nadu (illustrative, verify before public use)

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion clause — conditions diagnosed or treated within 48 months of policy commencement
decision_summary: Ombudsman found that the insurer's repudiation was based solely on a casual mention of 'blood pressure monitoring' in a routine check-up note, which did not constitute a diagnosis or treatment of hypertension under IRDAI guidelines.
successful_arguments: A mention of blood pressure monitoring in a general health check-up does not constitute a diagnosis of hypertension
Policyholder was never prescribed antihypertensive medication before policy inception
IRDAI circular on PED clarification: insurer must show actual diagnosis and treatment, not mere clinical observation
key_evidence: Routine health check-up report mentioning BP monitoring — no diagnosis note
Pharmacy records from pre-policy period showing no antihypertensive drugs purchased
Treating cardiologist's affidavit that formal hypertension diagnosis was made post policy inception
source_citation: Insurance Ombudsman, Tamil Nadu (synthetic case based on common Ombudsman ruling patterns)

relevant_policy_clause: Pre-existing disease exclusion — 4-year waiting period
decision_summary: Commission held that hypothyroidism managed through diet alone (no medication at policy start) did not trigger the PED disclosure obligation as the condition was subclinical and not under active medical treatment.
successful_arguments: Subclinical hypothyroidism not requiring medication is not a 'pre-existing disease' within the policy definition
IRDAI Health Insurance Regulations 2016 define PED as a condition requiring active medical treatment — diet management alone does not qualify
Policyholder disclosed all conditions for which they received medical treatment
key_evidence: Thyroid function test report from pre-policy period showing borderline TSH levels
No prescription or pharmacy records for thyroid medication pre-dating policy
Treating endocrinologist's note: medication commenced after policy start
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Gujarat (synthetic — based on documented IRDAI subclinical PED ruling precedents)

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion — conditions existing prior to policy commencement, waiting period 4 years
decision_summary: Commission upheld repudiation as the policyholder had undergone an angiography procedure 6 months before taking the policy — clear evidence of a known cardiac condition that was not disclosed in the proposal form.
failed_arguments: Policyholder argued the angiography was 'preventive' and no formal diagnosis of CAD was made — commission found the clinical documentation showed otherwise
Claim that insurer waived non-disclosure by accepting premium for 4 years was rejected as the waiting period had not yet elapsed
key_evidence: Angiography report dated 6 months before policy inception showing significant coronary stenosis
Cardiologist's referral letter for the angiography explicitly using 'suspected CAD' in diagnosis
source_citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Delhi (synthetic — consistent with documented NCDRC CAD non-disclosure patterns)

relevant_policy_clause: PED — respiratory conditions, 2-year waiting period
decision_summary: Ombudsman found that childhood asthma that had been in complete remission for over 10 years without any inhaler or medication use did not constitute a pre-existing disease requiring disclosure at the time of proposal.
successful_arguments: Asthma in complete remission for 10+ years without medication does not constitute an active pre-existing condition
Medical literature accepted by ombudsman: remission lasting more than 5 years with zero symptom recurrence is clinically equivalent to resolved condition
Policyholder disclosed all conditions for which they were currently receiving treatment
key_evidence: Childhood medical records showing last asthma treatment was 12 years before policy start
Treating pulmonologist's certificate: no asthma medication or inhaler prescribed in 10 years
Current hospital discharge citing an entirely separate trigger unrelated to childhood asthma history
source_citation: Insurance Ombudsman, Maharashtra (synthetic — based on IRDAI remission/dormancy PED guidelines)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for cataract surgery — Schedule of Benefits, Clause 3.2
decision_summary: Commission upheld waiting period application. Surgery was performed 18 months after policy commencement, which fell squarely within the 2-year waiting period for cataract. Policyholder's argument that the condition was 'urgent' was not substantiated by any medical certificate of urgency.
failed_arguments: Urgency argument rejected as no ophthalmologist certificate was produced claiming immediate surgical need
Argument that waiting periods are unfair was rejected — they are IRDAI-approved standard policy terms
key_evidence: Policy schedule showing cataract surgery in 2-year waiting period list
Hospital admission date: 18 months post policy start
No ophthalmologist urgency certificate on record
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Karnataka (synthetic — based on documented cataract waiting period rulings)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for hernia repair surgery
decision_summary: Ombudsman ruled that an inguinal hernia that presented acutely (strangulated, emergency surgery required) falls outside the waiting period exclusion because the emergency presentation was a new acute event, not a scheduled elective procedure.
successful_arguments: Strangulated hernia requiring emergency surgery is an acute emergency, not an elective procedure — the waiting period clause applies to elective planned surgeries
Treating surgeon's certificate confirmed emergency surgical intervention was necessary within hours of admission
No prior hernia diagnosis or treatment existed — this was the first presentation
key_evidence: Emergency admission note: patient presented with severe abdominal pain, irreducible hernia
Operating surgeon's certificate: immediate surgical intervention required to prevent intestinal necrosis
Prior medical records showing no hernia diagnosis or treatment
source_citation: Insurance Ombudsman, Delhi (synthetic — consistent with documented emergency surgery waiting period exception rulings)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for gallbladder surgery (cholecystectomy)
decision_summary: Waiting period clause clearly applied — cholecystectomy was an elective planned procedure performed 13 months into the policy. Policyholder knew about gallstones for 6 months before surgery and made no attempt to establish urgency.
failed_arguments: Policyholder argued pain episodes constituted urgency — commission found symptom management (conservative treatment) was ongoing for 6 months, negating urgency claim
Argument that waiting period information was not clearly communicated was rejected — policy brochure and schedule clearly listed gallstone surgery in exclusion table
key_evidence: Ultrasound report showing gallstones dated 6 months before surgery
GP's notes showing conservative symptom management over preceding months
Policy schedule with gallbladder surgery explicitly listed in waiting period table
source_citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Uttar Pradesh (synthetic)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for varicose vein procedures
decision_summary: Commission found waiting period applied to the surgical laser ablation procedure itself, but directed the insurer to pay for hospitalization costs, nursing, and pharmacy charges during the admission that were not directly attributable to the excluded surgery.
successful_arguments: Hospitalization overhead (room rent, nursing, medication, anaesthesia pre-assessment) is not synonymous with 'the procedure' under the waiting period clause
Insurer's blanket rejection of the entire claim was an overreach — the clause excludes the specific procedure, not all associated medical costs
failed_arguments: Claim that varicose veins constituted a vascular emergency was rejected as elective admission records showed pre-booked admission date 2 weeks prior
key_evidence: Itemized hospital bill separating procedure cost from hospitalization overhead
Elective pre-booked admission record
Policy clause language specifying 'varicose vein operations/procedures' — not 'all related hospitalization'
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kerala (synthetic — based on documented partial-relief pattern for waiting period cases)

relevant_policy_clause: Exclusion clause — dental treatment and surgery, unless arising from accidental bodily injury
decision_summary: Dental procedure (tooth extraction and crown work) fell squarely within the standard dental exclusion clause. Policyholder's argument that the dental issue was secondary to a jaw injury was not substantiated by accident records.
failed_arguments: Policyholder argued dental treatment was consequential to facial trauma — no accident FIR or contemporaneous medical record of injury was produced
Exclusion clause was clearly printed and explained in policy schedule
key_evidence: Hospital bill showing elective dental procedure codes
No FIR, accident report, or contemporaneous injury record
Policy schedule listing dental exclusion
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Andhra Pradesh (synthetic)

relevant_policy_clause: Claim processing — submission of originals of all hospital bills, discharge summary, and investigation reports within 30 days
decision_summary: Ombudsman found that the insurer's rejection of the claim solely on the basis of a delay in submitting original documents (caused by the hospital's administrative backlog) was not sustainable when the policyholder had submitted all documents within 60 days and had written to the insurer explaining the delay.
successful_arguments: Delay in obtaining original documents was attributable to hospital's administrative delay, not claimant's negligence
Policyholder proactively communicated delay reason to insurer in writing within 30 days
IRDAI guidelines: claim rejection solely on technical document delay grounds, without prejudice to the insurer, is not sustainable
key_evidence: Hospital letter confirming administrative backlog in issuing original discharge summaries
Policyholder's email to insurer within 30-day deadline explaining delay with timeline commitment
Complete original document set submitted on day 58
source_citation: Insurance Ombudsman, Karnataka (synthetic — based on IRDAI regulation 13 on document submission and documented Ombudsman patterns)

relevant_policy_clause: Room rent sub-limit: 1% of sum insured per day; ICU sub-limit: 2% of sum insured per day
decision_summary: Insurer applied proportionate deduction across all claim components due to room rent sub-limit breach. Commission held the proportionate deduction on post-ICU room components was correctly applied, but directed the insurer to pay full ICU costs as the ICU sub-limit was not breached.
successful_arguments: ICU charges should be assessed independently against the ICU sub-limit, not bundled with general room rent proportionate deduction
Proportionate deduction mechanism, while valid, must be applied component by component per IRDAI guidelines, not as a blanket deduction
failed_arguments: Argument that room rent sub-limits are unconscionable was rejected — IRDAI permits them and they were clearly disclosed
key_evidence: Itemized hospital bill showing ICU vs general ward costs separately
Policy schedule showing ICU sub-limit at 2% vs room rent sub-limit at 1%
Calculation sheet prepared by policyholder's counsel showing correct proportionate deduction methodology
source_citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Maharashtra (synthetic — based on documented sub-limit proportionate deduction rulings)

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion — 4-year waiting period
decision_summary: The insurer repudiated on the basis that a creatinine blood test result slightly above normal range 2 years before policy commencement indicated pre-existing kidney disease. National Commission held that a single borderline lab value — without a physician's diagnosis note, without treatment, and without a follow-up that confirmed kidney disease — was an insufficient basis to establish a PED under any reasonable clinical or legal standard.
successful_arguments: A borderline lab value without clinical follow-up or formal diagnosis does not constitute a pre-existing disease
Policyholder had no knowledge of any kidney condition — no physician ever communicated a diagnosis
Insurer's medical evaluator's opinion was based on retrospective interpretation of a single data point, which the commission found speculative
key_evidence: Single creatinine test report from 2 years before policy with no follow-up test or physician diagnosis note
Complete absence of any prescription, hospital visit, or treatment record for kidney disease pre-policy
Nephrologist's affidavit that the borderline value was within normal population variation and did not require clinical follow-up at that level
source_citation: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (synthetic — consistent with documented single lab value repudiation reversal patterns)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for piles/fistula/fissure surgical treatment
decision_summary: Commission found that the surgery was performed 18.5 months after policy start, which was within the waiting period. However, the insurer's failure to include piles surgery in the clearly communicated waiting period schedule (it was in internal underwriting notes but not the policyholder-facing policy document) meant the policyholder had no reasonable notice of this exclusion. Insurer was directed to pay the claim.
successful_arguments: Waiting period exclusions must be specifically communicated to the policyholder in the policy document — insurer cannot rely on exclusions in internal underwriting guidelines not shared with the policyholder
IRDAI Health Insurance Regulations 2016: all exclusions must be specifically enumerated in the policy document in a readable and accessible manner
key_evidence: Policyholder-facing policy schedule: piles surgery NOT listed in waiting period table
Insurer's internal underwriting file: piles listed in internal exclusion schedule
IRDAI Regulation 8: specific exclusion disclosure obligation
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Rajasthan (synthetic — based on documented exclusion non-disclosure ruling patterns)

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion — 4-year waiting period for pre-existing conditions
decision_summary: State Commission upheld repudiation. Policyholder had been admitted to a different hospital for jaundice and elevated liver enzymes 18 months before policy commencement and had received treatment. This constituted a known, treated liver condition that was not disclosed. Waiting period had not elapsed at time of claim.
failed_arguments: Policyholder argued jaundice was unrelated to cirrhosis — commission held clinical progression from documented liver disease to cirrhosis was a foreseeable and medically connected outcome that should have been disclosed
Argument that a 'different hospital' record should not be attributed to the policyholder was rejected
key_evidence: Discharge summary from prior hospitalization (18 months pre-policy): elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, clinical suspicion of liver pathology
Prescription for hepatoprotective medication from prior hospitalization
Current admission records confirming decompensated cirrhosis with documented disease progression
source_citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Telangana (synthetic)

relevant_policy_clause: Claim submission — treating surgeon's certificate required; internal fixation surgery requires pre-authorization
decision_summary: Ombudsman held that pre-authorization rejection due to emergency surgical circumstances (accident victim brought in unconscious, surgery required immediately) cannot be sustained. Emergency pre-authorization waiver provisions apply. Insurer directed to settle claim in full.
successful_arguments: Pre-authorization requirements are waived in genuine emergency situations per IRDAI emergency treatment guidelines
Patient was admitted unconscious following a road accident — obtaining pre-authorization was physically impossible
Hospital informed the insurer within 24 hours of admission, which met the emergency notification requirement
key_evidence: FIR and ambulance records showing emergency road accident admission
Treating surgeon's emergency certificate: surgery commenced within 2 hours of admission
Hospital's post-admission notification to insurer timestamped 20 hours after admission
source_citation: Insurance Ombudsman, Maharashtra (synthetic — based on documented emergency pre-auth waiver rulings)

relevant_policy_clause: Sum insured Rs. 5,00,000; co-payment 20% for claims above Rs. 3,00,000
decision_summary: Insurer applied co-payment incorrectly — co-payment clause required 20% co-pay on the amount exceeding Rs. 3,00,000, not 20% on the entire claim amount. Commission directed recomputation and additional payment of Rs. 38,000.
successful_arguments: Policy clause states '20% co-payment on the amount exceeding the threshold' — not on the full claim
Plain reading of the clause, as required by contra proferentem principle, favors the policyholder interpretation
Insurer's own policy wordings brochure contained an example that supported policyholder's calculation method
key_evidence: Policy document with exact co-payment clause wording
Insurer's own product brochure with calculation example
Policyholder's calculation worksheet showing correct vs. insurer's methodology
source_citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Karnataka (synthetic — based on contra proferentem and co-payment calculation dispute patterns)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for hysterectomy and fibroid removal procedures
decision_summary: Ombudsman upheld waiting period. Surgery performed 16.5 months into the policy, within the 2-year waiting period for fibroid procedures. No emergency surgical certificate was produced. Waiting period clause was clearly disclosed in the policy schedule and health card issued at inception.
failed_arguments: Policyholder argued severe menorrhagia constituted urgency — no gynaecologist certificate of emergent surgical need was submitted
Argument that gynaecological conditions should have shorter waiting periods was a policy design question outside ombudsman's jurisdiction
key_evidence: Policy schedule clearly listing fibroid removal in 2-year waiting period
Elective surgery booking records showing pre-booked OT date
No gynaecologist urgency certificate in claim file
source_citation: Insurance Ombudsman, Punjab (synthetic)
